nameStory: The slender meadow katydid gets its name from its notably thin, elongated body shape that distinguishes it from its more robust katydid cousins. Unlike the broad-leaf katydids that gave the whole family their famous "katy-did, katy-didn't" call, this grassland specialist has evolved a streamlined form perfect for navigating through dense meadow grasses.
description: The slender meadow katydid is a graceful, elongated green insect that looks like a delicate cross between a grasshopper and a cricket. These narrow-bodied katydids typically measure about an inch long and sport long, thread-like antennae that can be twice their body length. Their bright green coloration and slender build make them perfectly camouflaged among grass blades and meadow stems. Like other katydids, they're accomplished musicians, though their songs are much more subtle than their loud tree-dwelling relatives.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctively narrow and elongated body that feels delicate when gently handled, much thinner than typical grasshoppers

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Extremely long, hair-thin antennae that extend well beyond the body length and wave constantly as the insect moves

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Bright grass-green color that may have subtle brown or tan markings along the sides, providing perfect camouflage

idTips.label: Wings
idTips.description: Long, narrow wings that extend past the abdomen tip, with a papery texture and visible veining when viewed up close

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Moves with deliberate, slow motions through grass rather than the quick hops of grasshoppers, often swaying like a blade of grass

habitat: Look for slender meadow katydids in open grasslands, meadows, and prairie edges throughout New England's lower elevations. They prefer areas with tall grasses and wildflowers, often found in old fields, roadside ditches, and the grassy margins of wetlands. These katydids thrive in sunny, open spaces where native grasses dominate, avoiding heavily wooded areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs laid the previous fall remain dormant in soil and plant stems.
seasonality.summer: Young nymphs begin appearing in early summer, gradually developing through several molts. Peak activity occurs in late summer when adults become fully mature and most vocal.
seasonality.fall: Adults reach their peak numbers and calling activity in early fall, when mating and egg-laying occur before the first frost kills the adults.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs survive the winter, hidden in protected spots within grass stems and soil debris.

funFact: Unlike their famous "katy-did" calling cousins, slender meadow katydids produce their music by rapidly vibrating their wings to create ultrasonic frequencies mostly above human hearing range - they're having entire conversations we can barely detect!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with young grasshoppers, but remember that katydids have antennae longer than their bodies while grasshopper antennae are always shorter. The slender build and slow, deliberate movements also distinguish them from the quick-hopping grasshoppers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called katydids, meadow katydids like this species rarely make the classic "katy-did" sound that gave the family its name - that distinctive call comes from the broad-winged katydids that live in trees and shrubs, not these grassland specialists.
compareHints: Among New England's meadow katydids, the slender meadow katydid lives up to its name with the thinnest, most elongated body of the group. The short-winged meadow katydid has notably shorter wings that don't extend past its abdomen, while the saltmarsh species is restricted to coastal areas. The slender's long wings and inland grassland habitat help distinguish it from its meadow katydid relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its meadow katydid relatives, the short-winged species is immediately recognizable by its abbreviated wings - all other Conocephalus species in New England have long wings that extend to or beyond the tip of their abdomen.

Among New England's meadow katydids, the straight-lanced stands out for its perfectly straight wing edges - the short-winged has wings that don't extend past its body, the slender has curved wing edges, and the saltmarsh is found only in coastal salt marshes.

Unlike the Short-winged Meadow Katydid which has reduced wings and prefers wet meadows, or the Slender Meadow Katydid found in freshwater marshes, the Saltmarsh Meadow Katydid is distinguished by its exclusive salt marsh habitat and well-developed wings.
